questions.prompt: Which organelle is the main site of aerobic respiration in a eukaryotic cell?
options: Mitochondrion
Ribosome
Golgi apparatus
Lysosome
questions.correctAnswer: Mitochondrion
questions.explanation: Mitochondria contain enzymes that release usable energy from food during aerobic respiration.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify organelles and relate their structure to cell functions.

questions.prompt: Which cell structure is directly involved in protein synthesis?
options: Ribosome
Vacuole
Cell wall
Centrosome
questions.correctAnswer: Ribosome
questions.explanation: Ribosomes translate genetic information into chains of amino acids that form proteins.
questions.learningOutcome: State the functions of major cell structures in plant and animal cells.

questions.prompt: What property of the cell membrane allows some substances to pass while restricting others?
options: Selective permeability
Rigid impermeability
Complete solubility
Permanent contraction
questions.correctAnswer: Selective permeability
questions.explanation: The membrane regulates entry and exit because its phospholipid layer and proteins allow only certain substances through.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe how the cell membrane controls movement of substances.

questions.prompt: Why does an enzyme act on a specific substrate?
options: Its active site has a complementary shape to the substrate
It changes into any shape needed by the cell
It is always used up during the reaction
It only works when no substrate is present
questions.correctAnswer: Its active site has a complementary shape to the substrate
questions.explanation: Specificity occurs because the substrate fits the enzyme active site and forms an enzyme-substrate complex.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain enzyme specificity using the active site model.

questions.prompt: Which reagent is commonly used to test for reducing sugars such as glucose?
options: Benedict's solution
Iodine solution
Biuret reagent
Ethanol emulsion
questions.correctAnswer: Benedict's solution
questions.explanation: Benedict's solution changes colour when heated with reducing sugars, indicating their presence.
questions.learningOutcome: Select appropriate food-test reagents for biological molecules.

questions.prompt: A pancreatic cell secretes many digestive enzymes. Which organelle would be especially abundant in this cell?
options: Rough endoplasmic reticulum
Contractile vacuole
Chloroplast
Cell wall
questions.correctAnswer: Rough endoplasmic reticulum
questions.explanation: Rough endoplasmic reticulum has ribosomes that make proteins for secretion, including many enzymes.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate organelle abundance to specialised cell function.

questions.prompt: What is the most likely result when a red blood cell is placed in a very concentrated salt solution?
options: It loses water and shrinks
It gains water and bursts
It forms a cell wall
It begins photosynthesis
questions.correctAnswer: It loses water and shrinks
questions.explanation: Water moves out of the cell by osmosis because the surrounding solution has a lower water potential.
questions.learningOutcome: Predict osmotic effects on animal cells in solutions of different concentration.

questions.prompt: Why do plant cells become turgid when placed in dilute solution?
options: Water enters the vacuole by osmosis and the cell wall resists bursting
Minerals leave the cytoplasm by active transport
The nucleus absorbs starch grains directly
The chloroplasts release oxygen into the vacuole
questions.correctAnswer: Water enters the vacuole by osmosis and the cell wall resists bursting
questions.explanation: Osmotic water gain expands the vacuole, and the rigid wall creates turgor pressure.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain turgor in plant cells using osmosis and cell-wall support.

questions.prompt: Which comparison between rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum is accurate?
options: Rough ER has ribosomes for protein synthesis, while smooth ER is involved in lipid metabolism
Rough ER stores genetic material, while smooth ER makes chromosomes
Rough ER digests old organelles, while smooth ER controls mitosis
Rough ER performs photosynthesis, while smooth ER absorbs light
questions.correctAnswer: Rough ER has ribosomes for protein synthesis, while smooth ER is involved in lipid metabolism
questions.explanation: Ribosomes on rough ER support protein synthesis, while smooth ER has roles in lipid production and detoxification.
questions.learningOutcome: Compare related organelles by structure and function.

questions.prompt: A cell image is 60 mm long on a micrograph, while the actual cell is 0.15 mm long. What is the magnification?
options: 400 times
40 times
9 times
0.0025 times
questions.correctAnswer: 400 times
questions.explanation: Magnification equals image size divided by actual size, so 60 divided by 0.15 is 400.
questions.learningOutcome: Calculate magnification using image size and actual specimen size.

questions.prompt: In a dialysis-tubing experiment, glucose appears in the surrounding water but starch remains inside the tubing. What does this show?
options: Small glucose molecules diffused through the membrane, but larger starch molecules did not
Starch changed into cellulose outside the tubing
The membrane actively pumped starch into the water
Water destroyed all glucose inside the tubing
questions.correctAnswer: Small glucose molecules diffused through the membrane, but larger starch molecules did not
questions.explanation: Partially permeable membranes allow some small molecules to pass while restricting larger molecules.
questions.learningOutcome: Interpret simple experiments that model diffusion through membranes.

questions.prompt: Root hair cells absorb nitrate ions from soil even when nitrate concentration is lower in the soil than in the cell. Which process is required?
options: Active transport
Simple diffusion
Osmosis
Evaporation
questions.correctAnswer: Active transport
questions.explanation: Moving ions against their concentration gradient requires energy supplied by respiration.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply the idea of concentration gradients to active transport in living cells.

questions.prompt: A protease works fastest at pH 2 and slowly at pH 7. Which conclusion is most reasonable?
options: The protease is adapted to an acidic environment such as the stomach
The protease has no optimum pH
Neutral pH permanently increases its activity
The enzyme can only digest carbohydrates
questions.correctAnswer: The protease is adapted to an acidic environment such as the stomach
questions.explanation: Enzymes have optimum pH values; pepsin-like proteases work best in acidic conditions.
questions.learningOutcome: Interpret enzyme activity data in relation to pH and biological location.

questions.prompt: Why do very small cells exchange materials more efficiently than very large cells of the same shape?
options: They have a larger surface-area-to-volume ratio
They contain no cytoplasm
They do not need a cell membrane
They use DNA as a respiratory surface
questions.correctAnswer: They have a larger surface-area-to-volume ratio
questions.explanation: A higher surface-area-to-volume ratio gives more membrane area per unit volume for diffusion and exchange.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate cell size to efficiency of material exchange.

questions.prompt: A cell has many Golgi bodies, rough ER, and vesicles. What function is it most likely specialised for?
options: Producing and secreting proteins
Storing dry seeds
Conducting water as a dead tube
Absorbing light with chlorophyll
questions.correctAnswer: Producing and secreting proteins
questions.explanation: Rough ER makes proteins, Golgi bodies modify and package them, and vesicles move them for secretion.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse organelle patterns to infer specialised cell function.

questions.prompt: Potato strips are placed in several sucrose solutions. Which observation best identifies the isotonic solution?
options: The strip shows no net change in mass
The strip becomes green
The solution changes from clear to blue-black
The strip releases oxygen bubbles
questions.correctAnswer: The strip shows no net change in mass
questions.explanation: In an isotonic solution, water enters and leaves cells at equal rates, so there is no net mass change.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse experimental results to identify isotonic conditions in plant tissue.

questions.prompt: A high fever can make some enzyme-controlled reactions less efficient. Which explanation best accounts for this?
options: Heat can alter the active-site shape and reduce substrate binding
Heat changes all enzymes into carbohydrates
Heat removes the need for catalysts
Heat makes substrates unable to collide
questions.correctAnswer: Heat can alter the active-site shape and reduce substrate binding
questions.explanation: Excessive heat can denature enzyme proteins, changing the active site and lowering activity.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse how temperature affects enzyme structure and activity.

questions.prompt: Which plan best tests the effect of temperature on amylase activity?
options: Use equal starch and amylase volumes at different temperatures, then time how long starch takes to disappear
Use different enzymes, different pH values, and different starch volumes in every tube
Heat one tube only and record its colour before adding starch
Mix iodine with amylase and avoid measuring time or temperature
questions.correctAnswer: Use equal starch and amylase volumes at different temperatures, then time how long starch takes to disappear
questions.explanation: A fair test changes temperature while keeping other variables constant and measuring reaction rate.
questions.learningOutcome: Design a controlled experiment to investigate factors affecting enzyme activity.

questions.prompt: What is the main role of chlorophyll in photosynthesis?
options: Absorbing light energy
Transporting oxygen in blood
Digesting proteins
Breaking down urea
questions.correctAnswer: Absorbing light energy
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll captures light energy that drives the conversion of carbon dioxide and water into carbohydrates.
questions.learningOutcome: State the role of chlorophyll in photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Which vascular tissue transports water and mineral salts from roots to leaves?
options: Xylem
Phloem
Cambium
Epidermis
questions.correctAnswer: Xylem
questions.explanation: Xylem vessels conduct water and dissolved mineral salts upwards through the plant.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify tissues involved in transport of water and minerals in plants.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of bile in digestion?
options: Emulsifying fats into small droplets
Digesting starch into maltose
Absorbing amino acids into blood
Producing hydrochloric acid
questions.correctAnswer: Emulsifying fats into small droplets
questions.explanation: Bile increases the surface area of fats so lipase can digest them more efficiently.
questions.learningOutcome: State the function of bile in fat digestion.

questions.prompt: How do villi in the small intestine improve absorption?
options: They provide a large surface area and a rich blood supply
They grind food into smaller particles
They prevent enzymes from mixing with food
They produce all the bile used in digestion
questions.correctAnswer: They provide a large surface area and a rich blood supply
questions.explanation: Villi are folded projections with capillaries and lacteals that increase nutrient absorption.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain adaptations of the small intestine for absorption.

questions.prompt: Why are stomata important for photosynthesis?
options: They allow carbon dioxide to diffuse into the leaf
They pump sucrose from roots into flowers
They digest excess chlorophyll
They prevent all water movement in plants
questions.correctAnswer: They allow carbon dioxide to diffuse into the leaf
questions.explanation: Open stomata permit carbon dioxide entry for photosynthesis and allow oxygen and water vapour to leave.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the role of stomata in gas exchange during photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Which factor can limit photosynthesis when light and water are plentiful?
options: Carbon dioxide concentration
Number of red blood cells
Amount of bile in the liver
Thickness of tooth enamel
questions.correctAnswer: Carbon dioxide concentration
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis needs carbon dioxide; when it is scarce, the rate can remain low even with enough light and water.
questions.learningOutcome: Recognise limiting factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: A maize plant has yellowing older leaves and poor growth because it lacks a key mineral for amino acid synthesis. Which mineral is most likely deficient?
options: Nitrate
Calcium carbonate
Sodium chloride
Silica
questions.correctAnswer: Nitrate
questions.explanation: Nitrate supplies nitrogen used to make amino acids, proteins, and chlorophyll-containing tissues.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate mineral nutrients to plant growth and deficiency symptoms.

questions.prompt: Which digestive enzyme begins starch digestion in the human mouth?
options: Salivary amylase
Pepsin
Lipase
Trypsin
questions.correctAnswer: Salivary amylase
questions.explanation: Salivary amylase starts breaking starch into smaller sugars while food is chewed.
questions.learningOutcome: Match digestive enzymes with their substrates and sites of action.

questions.prompt: A root hair cell has a long projection and many mitochondria. Which function do these adaptations support?
options: Absorbing water and mineral ions from soil
Producing pollen grains for fertilisation
Transporting oxygen in animal blood
Emulsifying fats in the duodenum
questions.correctAnswer: Absorbing water and mineral ions from soil
questions.explanation: The long projection increases surface area, and mitochondria supply energy for active mineral uptake.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply cell adaptation concepts to mineral and water uptake in plants.

questions.prompt: In a starch test on a leaf, why is the leaf first boiled in ethanol after being placed in hot water?
options: To remove chlorophyll so the iodine colour change can be seen
To add glucose to the leaf cells
To kill bacteria that produce starch
To seal the stomata permanently
questions.correctAnswer: To remove chlorophyll so the iodine colour change can be seen
questions.explanation: Ethanol extracts chlorophyll, making it easier to observe the blue-black colour produced by starch and iodine.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain procedures used in testing leaves for starch.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes translocation in a flowering plant?
options: Movement of sugars through phloem from sources to sinks
Movement of water through xylem from leaves to roots only
Movement of oxygen through stomata into soil
Movement of bile through the small intestine
questions.correctAnswer: Movement of sugars through phloem from sources to sinks
questions.explanation: Translocation moves sucrose and other organic solutes in phloem from producing or storage regions to areas of use.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply source-sink ideas to transport of manufactured food in plants.

questions.prompt: Crop roots in waterlogged soil often absorb fewer mineral ions. What is the best explanation?
options: Less oxygen is available for respiration needed in active transport
Waterlogged soil contains no water for osmosis
The leaves stop making chlorophyll immediately
All mineral ions become proteins in the soil
questions.correctAnswer: Less oxygen is available for respiration needed in active transport
questions.explanation: Mineral uptake often needs ATP, and low oxygen reduces aerobic respiration in root cells.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain how soil aeration affects active uptake of minerals.

questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly shows the main chemical digestion of proteins in humans?
options: Proteins to peptides to amino acids
Proteins to starch to glucose
Proteins to fatty acids to glycerol
Proteins to oxygen to carbon dioxide
questions.correctAnswer: Proteins to peptides to amino acids
questions.explanation: Proteases first split proteins into shorter peptides and then into amino acids for absorption.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply knowledge of digestive enzymes to nutrient breakdown pathways.

questions.prompt: In a photosynthesis experiment, the oxygen bubbles from pondweed increase as lamp distance decreases. What does this indicate?
options: Higher light intensity increased the photosynthesis rate
Lower light intensity increased respiration only
Pondweed stopped using carbon dioxide
Oxygen bubbles show protein digestion
questions.correctAnswer: Higher light intensity increased the photosynthesis rate
questions.explanation: Moving the lamp closer raises light intensity, which can increase photosynthesis when light is limiting.
questions.learningOutcome: Interpret experimental evidence for light intensity as a limiting factor.

questions.prompt: A plant has pale young leaves while older leaves remain greener. Which explanation is most consistent with iron deficiency?
options: Iron is needed for chlorophyll formation and is not easily moved from older leaves
Iron is the main sugar transported in phloem
Iron directly forms all plant cell walls
Iron closes stomata during the night
questions.correctAnswer: Iron is needed for chlorophyll formation and is not easily moved from older leaves
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency often appears first in younger leaves because iron is relatively immobile in the plant.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse plant deficiency symptoms using mineral function and mobility.

questions.prompt: A graph of photosynthesis rate rises with light intensity, then levels off. Which inference is most likely after the graph levels off?
options: Another factor such as carbon dioxide concentration has become limiting
Photosynthesis has changed into digestion
Light has stopped entering the leaf completely
Chlorophyll has become an animal pigment
questions.correctAnswer: Another factor such as carbon dioxide concentration has become limiting
questions.explanation: When increasing light no longer raises the rate, a different factor is limiting the reaction.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse limiting-factor graphs for photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Why can cattle obtain energy from cellulose-rich grass more effectively than humans?
options: Microorganisms in the rumen digest cellulose into usable products
Cattle bile contains oxygen for photosynthesis
Human villi are absent from the small intestine
Grass cellulose is already glucose before chewing
questions.correctAnswer: Microorganisms in the rumen digest cellulose into usable products
questions.explanation: Ruminants host microbes that produce cellulase and break down cellulose during fermentation.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse adaptations of ruminants for feeding on cellulose-rich diets.

questions.prompt: A school greenhouse has healthy tomato plants but low yield during cloudy weeks. Which intervention best targets the likely limiting factor?
options: Provide controlled supplementary light while maintaining water and carbon dioxide supply
Remove all leaves to reduce water loss
Stop ventilation permanently to trap stale air
Apply only table salt around the roots
questions.correctAnswer: Provide controlled supplementary light while maintaining water and carbon dioxide supply
questions.explanation: Cloudy weather reduces light intensity, so controlled lighting can raise photosynthesis if other needs are met.
questions.learningOutcome: Propose evidence-based ways to improve plant productivity under controlled conditions.

questions.prompt: Which blood pigment transports most oxygen in human blood?
options: Haemoglobin
Chlorophyll
Melanin
Bile pigment
questions.correctAnswer: Haemoglobin
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin in red blood cells binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it to body tissues.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify blood components and their functions in transport.

questions.prompt: Which feature helps arteries withstand high blood pressure?
options: Thick elastic muscular walls
Valves along their whole length
One-cell-thick walls
Large air spaces filled with oxygen
questions.correctAnswer: Thick elastic muscular walls
questions.explanation: Arteries receive blood directly from the heart, so their thick elastic walls withstand and smooth pressure changes.
questions.learningOutcome: State structural adaptations of blood vessels.

questions.prompt: What is the main gas-exchange surface in human lungs?
options: Alveoli
Tracheal cartilage
Diaphragm muscle
Nasal hair
questions.correctAnswer: Alveoli
questions.explanation: Alveoli provide a thin, moist, large surface area where oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify respiratory structures involved in gas exchange.

questions.prompt: Why are capillary walls only one cell thick?
options: They shorten the diffusion distance between blood and tissues
They pump blood faster than the heart
They prevent all exchange with tissues
They store oxygen as starch
questions.correctAnswer: They shorten the diffusion distance between blood and tissues
questions.explanation: Thin capillary walls allow rapid diffusion of gases, nutrients, and wastes.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain capillary adaptations for exchange.

questions.prompt: What is the function of valves in veins?
options: Preventing backflow of blood
Producing red blood cells
Adding oxygen to blood
Breaking down lactic acid
questions.correctAnswer: Preventing backflow of blood
questions.explanation: Venous blood flows at lower pressure, so valves help keep it moving towards the heart.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain how vein structure supports blood return to the heart.

questions.prompt: Which force mainly helps pull water upward through xylem during transpiration?
options: Cohesion and tension in the water column
Active pumping by red blood cells
Bile secretion from leaves
Digestion of cellulose in flowers
questions.correctAnswer: Cohesion and tension in the water column
questions.explanation: Evaporation from leaves creates tension, and cohesion keeps water molecules linked in the xylem stream.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the transpiration pull mechanism in xylem transport.

questions.prompt: During vigorous exercise, muscle cells may respire anaerobically. Which product accumulates in human muscles?
options: Lactic acid
Ethanol
Starch
Urea crystals
questions.correctAnswer: Lactic acid
questions.explanation: When oxygen supply is insufficient, muscles convert glucose to lactic acid and release less energy.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells.

questions.prompt: What happens to the diaphragm during inhalation?
options: It contracts and flattens, increasing chest volume
It relaxes and domes upward, decreasing chest volume
It secretes mucus into the alveoli
It pumps blood into the aorta
questions.correctAnswer: It contracts and flattens, increasing chest volume
questions.explanation: A flattened diaphragm increases thoracic volume, lowering pressure so air enters the lungs.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain how diaphragm movement changes thoracic volume during breathing.

questions.prompt: Which pathway correctly traces blood from the vena cava to the lungs?
options: Right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs
Left atrium, left ventricle, aorta, lungs
Right ventricle, left atrium, pulmonary vein, lungs
Aorta, right atrium, pulmonary vein, lungs
questions.correctAnswer: Right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs
questions.explanation: Deoxygenated blood returns to the right side of the heart and travels to the lungs through the pulmonary artery.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply knowledge of heart chambers and vessels to blood-flow pathways.

questions.prompt: Why does breathing rate remain high for a short time after sprinting?
options: Extra oxygen is needed to break down accumulated lactic acid
The lungs are making starch from glucose
The heart stops pumping during recovery
Muscles need to convert oxygen into bile
questions.correctAnswer: Extra oxygen is needed to break down accumulated lactic acid
questions.explanation: The body repays oxygen debt by supplying oxygen for recovery processes after anaerobic respiration.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply the concept of oxygen debt to exercise recovery.

questions.prompt: On a humid day, a leafy plant loses water more slowly. Which reason best explains this?
options: The water vapour gradient between leaf air spaces and outside air is reduced
The xylem changes into phloem
The roots stop absorbing all minerals
The leaves stop containing stomata
questions.correctAnswer: The water vapour gradient between leaf air spaces and outside air is reduced
questions.explanation: High humidity lowers the diffusion gradient for water vapour, reducing transpiration rate.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply diffusion gradients to environmental effects on transpiration.

questions.prompt: A learner with low haemoglobin feels tired after mild exercise. Which explanation links the symptom to transport?
options: Less oxygen is delivered to respiring tissues, reducing aerobic energy release
More bile is delivered to the lungs, increasing fat digestion
Blood plasma stops carrying glucose to cells
Capillaries become too thick for any blood flow
questions.correctAnswer: Less oxygen is delivered to respiring tissues, reducing aerobic energy release
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin carries oxygen, so reduced haemoglobin can lower oxygen supply for aerobic respiration.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply blood composition knowledge to explain oxygen-transport symptoms.

questions.prompt: In a potometer, what does movement of the air bubble mainly estimate?
options: Rate of water uptake by the shoot
Rate of food digestion in leaves
Rate of oxygen release by roots
Rate of mineral formation in soil
questions.correctAnswer: Rate of water uptake by the shoot
questions.explanation: A potometer estimates transpiration indirectly by measuring how quickly a shoot takes up water.
questions.learningOutcome: Use potometer observations to estimate water uptake and transpiration.

questions.prompt: A ring of bark is removed from a woody stem, but the xylem is left intact. What is most likely to build up above the ring?
options: Sugars transported in phloem
Water transported in xylem
Oxygen transported by haemoglobin
Urea transported from kidneys
questions.correctAnswer: Sugars transported in phloem
questions.explanation: Removing bark interrupts phloem, so sugars made in leaves accumulate above the removed ring.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse ring-barking evidence for phloem transport.

questions.prompt: People living at high altitude often have increased red blood cell production. What advantage does this provide?
options: It increases the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity in low-oxygen air
It prevents any need for breathing
It converts carbon dioxide into starch
It stops all diffusion in the lungs
questions.correctAnswer: It increases the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity in low-oxygen air
questions.explanation: More red blood cells can carry more haemoglobin, improving oxygen transport where oxygen availability is lower.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse physiological adaptation to environmental oxygen availability.

questions.prompt: Which observation would best support the idea that alveoli are adapted for rapid diffusion?
options: They are numerous, thin-walled, moist, and surrounded by capillaries
They have thick cartilage rings and no blood supply
They contain bile salts for fat emulsification
They are lined by waterproof cuticle like leaves
questions.correctAnswer: They are numerous, thin-walled, moist, and surrounded by capillaries
questions.explanation: Large surface area, short diffusion distance, moisture, and blood flow maintain efficient gas exchange.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse structural adaptations of respiratory surfaces for diffusion.

questions.prompt: A spirometer trace shows tidal volume rising during exercise. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options: Each breath moves a larger volume of air to meet greater oxygen demand
The lungs have stopped exchanging gases
The diaphragm no longer contracts
Blood pressure has become zero
questions.correctAnswer: Each breath moves a larger volume of air to meet greater oxygen demand
questions.explanation: During exercise, ventilation increases by raising breathing rate and often the volume of air per breath.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse breathing data in relation to exercise and cellular respiration.

questions.prompt: Which investigation best compares the effect of wind speed on transpiration?
options: Use the same leafy shoot in a potometer, vary only fan speed, and record bubble movement per minute
Use different plant species, different temperatures, and different leaf areas in every trial
Measure only soil colour before and after watering
Keep the plant in darkness and change both humidity and wind speed together
questions.correctAnswer: Use the same leafy shoot in a potometer, vary only fan speed, and record bubble movement per minute
questions.explanation: A controlled comparison changes wind speed while keeping other variables constant and measuring water uptake rate.
questions.learningOutcome: Design a fair test for environmental factors affecting transpiration.

questions.prompt: What is the functional unit of the kidney?
options: Nephron
Alveolus
Villus
Neuron
questions.correctAnswer: Nephron
questions.explanation: The nephron filters blood and adjusts filtrate to form urine.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify the nephron as the kidney unit responsible for urine formation.

questions.prompt: Which hormone lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake and storage of glucose?
options: Insulin
Adrenaline
Thyroxine
Oestrogen
questions.correctAnswer: Insulin
questions.explanation: Insulin stimulates cells to take up glucose and promotes conversion of glucose to glycogen in the liver and muscles.
questions.learningOutcome: State the role of insulin in blood glucose regulation.

questions.prompt: Which skin response helps cool the body on a hot day?
options: Sweat evaporation
Hair erection
Reduced blood flow to skin
Shivering
questions.correctAnswer: Sweat evaporation
questions.explanation: Evaporation of sweat removes heat from the skin surface and helps lower body temperature.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify body responses involved in temperature control.

questions.prompt: How does antidiuretic hormone help conserve water?
options: It increases water reabsorption in kidney tubules
It digests proteins in the stomach
It makes the liver produce bile
It prevents glucose from entering cells
questions.correctAnswer: It increases water reabsorption in kidney tubules
questions.explanation: ADH makes collecting ducts more permeable to water, producing a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the role of ADH in regulating body water levels.

questions.prompt: Which substances are normally present in glomerular filtrate but not in healthy urine after reabsorption?
options: Glucose and most amino acids
Large plasma proteins and red blood cells
Sand and cellulose
Oxygen bubbles and bile salts only
questions.correctAnswer: Glucose and most amino acids
questions.explanation: Small useful molecules enter the filtrate but are selectively reabsorbed in the nephron.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain selective reabsorption of useful substances in the nephron.

questions.prompt: What happens during deamination in the liver?
options: Excess amino acids are converted into urea and other products
Glucose is changed into oxygen
Bile is converted into red blood cells
Water is turned into glycogen
questions.correctAnswer: Excess amino acids are converted into urea and other products
questions.explanation: The liver removes amino groups from excess amino acids and converts the nitrogenous waste into urea.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe the role of the liver in nitrogenous waste formation.

questions.prompt: Why is blood glucose regulation described as negative feedback?
options: A change triggers responses that return glucose level toward normal
All hormones permanently increase glucose
The body ignores changes in glucose level
Glucose is always removed completely from blood
questions.correctAnswer: A change triggers responses that return glucose level toward normal
questions.explanation: Negative feedback reduces the original change and helps maintain a stable internal environment.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain negative feedback in maintaining internal stability.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of vasoconstriction in skin arterioles during cold conditions?
options: Less warm blood reaches the skin surface, reducing heat loss
More sweat evaporates from the skin
The body produces bile faster
The kidneys stop filtering blood completely
questions.correctAnswer: Less warm blood reaches the skin surface, reducing heat loss
questions.explanation: Narrower skin arterioles reduce blood flow near the surface and conserve body heat.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the role of blood vessels in conserving heat.

questions.prompt: After a long walk in hot weather without enough water, a learner produces little dark urine. What is the best explanation?
options: More ADH caused greater water reabsorption in the kidneys
The kidneys stopped making filtrate permanently
The liver converted urine into sweat
Glucose replaced all water in the blood
questions.correctAnswer: More ADH caused greater water reabsorption in the kidneys
questions.explanation: Dehydration raises ADH release, so more water is reabsorbed and urine becomes more concentrated.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply ADH regulation to explain urine concentration during dehydration.

questions.prompt: Blood glucose rises after a meal rich in ugali and beans. Which response helps restore normal glucose level?
options: Pancreas releases insulin and the liver stores glucose as glycogen
Pancreas releases less insulin and the liver releases more glucose
Kidneys convert glucose into oxygen
Skin arterioles constrict to store glucose
questions.correctAnswer: Pancreas releases insulin and the liver stores glucose as glycogen
questions.explanation: Insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage, reducing blood glucose after carbohydrate digestion.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply hormone control to blood glucose changes after meals.

questions.prompt: Which feature of dialysis tubing allows it to remove urea from blood but retain blood cells?
options: It is partially permeable to small solutes but not to cells
It actively produces new nephrons
It digests red blood cells into amino acids
It pumps glucose into the liver
questions.correctAnswer: It is partially permeable to small solutes but not to cells
questions.explanation: Dialysis membranes allow small wastes such as urea to diffuse out while larger cells and proteins remain in the blood.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply membrane permeability ideas to dialysis treatment.

questions.prompt: During a hot afternoon, which coordinated response helps prevent body temperature from rising too high?
options: Vasodilation and sweating increase heat loss
Shivering and vasoconstriction increase heat gain
ADH stops all kidney function
Insulin converts sweat into glycogen
questions.correctAnswer: Vasodilation and sweating increase heat loss
questions.explanation: More blood near the skin and evaporation of sweat both help remove heat from the body.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply thermoregulatory responses to hot environmental conditions.

questions.prompt: A urine test repeatedly shows glucose in urine. Which condition should be investigated by a qualified health worker?
options: Poor blood glucose regulation such as diabetes mellitus
Normal complete reabsorption of glucose
Absence of all filtration in kidneys
Excess chlorophyll in blood plasma
questions.correctAnswer: Poor blood glucose regulation such as diabetes mellitus
questions.explanation: Glucose in urine can occur when blood glucose exceeds the kidney's reabsorption capacity.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply knowledge of reabsorption and glucose regulation to urine-test results.

questions.prompt: Why is active transport important in selective reabsorption of glucose in the kidney tubule?
options: It can move glucose from filtrate into blood even against a concentration gradient
It changes glucose into urea before excretion
It filters red blood cells through the glomerulus
It prevents any water from being reabsorbed
questions.correctAnswer: It can move glucose from filtrate into blood even against a concentration gradient
questions.explanation: Useful substances such as glucose may be reclaimed from filtrate using carrier proteins and energy.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse how transport mechanisms support selective reabsorption.

questions.prompt: A runner overheats more easily on a hot humid day than on a hot dry day. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: High humidity reduces sweat evaporation, so less heat is removed
High humidity prevents blood from carrying oxygen at all
Sweat evaporates faster when the air is already saturated
The liver stops producing urea in humid air
questions.correctAnswer: High humidity reduces sweat evaporation, so less heat is removed
questions.explanation: When air contains much water vapour, sweat evaporates slowly and cooling becomes less effective.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse environmental effects on body cooling mechanisms.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly links a homeostatic organ with its regulated variable?
options: Pancreas - blood glucose level
Alveolus - amino acid sequence
Villus - body temperature set point
Ribosome - urine water content
questions.correctAnswer: Pancreas - blood glucose level
questions.explanation: The pancreas releases hormones such as insulin and glucagon that help regulate blood glucose.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse links between homeostatic organs and controlled variables.

questions.prompt: Blood glucose falls below normal during prolonged exercise. Which feedback response best helps restore it?
options: Glucagon promotes breakdown of liver glycogen to release glucose
Insulin promotes more glucose storage as glycogen
ADH converts urea into glucose
Sweat glands absorb glucose from the air
questions.correctAnswer: Glucagon promotes breakdown of liver glycogen to release glucose
questions.explanation: Glucagon raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogen breakdown and glucose release from the liver.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse negative feedback responses when blood glucose drops.

questions.prompt: Which plan is the safest classroom investigation of hydration effects on urine concentration?
options: Use prepared simulated urine samples of different concentrations and compare colour or specific gravity
Ask learners to avoid water for a whole day before testing themselves
Collect anonymous medical samples without consent
Add glucose to drinking water and diagnose classmates
questions.correctAnswer: Use prepared simulated urine samples of different concentrations and compare colour or specific gravity
questions.explanation: Simulated samples avoid health and privacy risks while still allowing learners to study concentration differences.
questions.learningOutcome: Design safe and ethical investigations of osmoregulation concepts.

questions.prompt: Which type of cell division produces gametes with half the normal chromosome number?
options: Meiosis
Mitosis
Binary fission
Budding
questions.correctAnswer: Meiosis
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number so gametes can fuse and restore the diploid number at fertilisation.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify meiosis as the division that produces haploid gametes.

questions.prompt: Which molecule carries hereditary information in most living organisms?
options: DNA
Starch
Cellulose
Bile
questions.correctAnswer: DNA
questions.explanation: DNA stores genetic instructions in sequences of nucleotide bases.
questions.learningOutcome: State the molecule responsible for carrying genetic information.

questions.prompt: What is pollination in flowering plants?
options: Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma
Fusion of two nuclei in the ovule
Growth of a seed into a seedling
Production of glucose in leaves
questions.correctAnswer: Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma
questions.explanation: Pollination moves pollen grains to the stigma, where fertilisation may later occur.
questions.learningOutcome: Define pollination in flowering plants.

questions.prompt: What is an allele?
options: An alternative form of a gene
A complete set of all body organs
A type of digestive enzyme
A mineral salt absorbed by roots
questions.correctAnswer: An alternative form of a gene
questions.explanation: Alleles are different versions of the same gene that can produce variation in a trait.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain basic genetic terms used in inheritance.

questions.prompt: In a heterozygous organism with genotype Tt, which allele is expressed if T is dominant?
options: Dominant allele T
Recessive allele t
Both alleles disappear
Neither allele is inherited
questions.correctAnswer: Dominant allele T
questions.explanation: A dominant allele is expressed in the phenotype even when paired with a recessive allele.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain dominance in heterozygous genotypes.

questions.prompt: Why does fertilisation restore the diploid chromosome number?
options: Two haploid gamete nuclei fuse
One diploid cell divides into four diploid cells
The placenta produces chromosomes
Pollen grains digest chromosomes
questions.correctAnswer: Two haploid gamete nuclei fuse
questions.explanation: Each gamete contributes one set of chromosomes, giving the zygote two sets after fusion.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain how fertilisation restores chromosome number.

questions.prompt: Which function is performed by the placenta during mammalian pregnancy?
options: Exchange of nutrients, gases, and wastes between mother and foetus
Production of pollen tubes
Digestion of cellulose in the rumen
Filtration of urine in the nephron
questions.correctAnswer: Exchange of nutrients, gases, and wastes between mother and foetus
questions.explanation: The placenta supports exchange while keeping maternal and foetal blood mostly separate.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the role of the placenta in foetal development.

questions.prompt: Which base pairing is correct in DNA?
options: Adenine pairs with thymine
Adenine pairs with cytosine
Guanine pairs with thymine
Uracil pairs with thymine
questions.correctAnswer: Adenine pairs with thymine
questions.explanation: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine, while cytosine pairs with guanine.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe complementary base pairing in DNA.

questions.prompt: In a monohybrid cross Aa x Aa, what proportion of offspring is expected to be homozygous recessive?
options: 1 out of 4
2 out of 4
3 out of 4
4 out of 4
questions.correctAnswer: 1 out of 4
questions.explanation: The possible genotypes are AA, Aa, Aa, and aa, so one quarter are homozygous recessive.
questions.learningOutcome: Use a Punnett square to predict genotype proportions in a monohybrid cross.

questions.prompt: How does crossing over during meiosis increase variation?
options: It exchanges chromosome segments between homologous chromosomes
It makes all gametes genetically identical
It removes DNA from every chromosome
It prevents fertilisation from occurring
questions.correctAnswer: It exchanges chromosome segments between homologous chromosomes
questions.explanation: Crossing over creates new combinations of alleles in gametes.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply the process of crossing over to explain genetic variation.

questions.prompt: Which chromosome combination usually produces a human male?
options: XY
XX
YY
XO only
questions.correctAnswer: XY
questions.explanation: A typical human male has one X chromosome and one Y chromosome in body cells.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply sex chromosome inheritance to human sex determination.

questions.prompt: A tall pea plant of unknown genotype is crossed with a short homozygous recessive plant. What is this type of cross called?
options: Test cross
Back diffusion
Binary fission
Double fertilisation
questions.correctAnswer: Test cross
questions.explanation: A test cross uses a homozygous recessive parent to reveal the genotype of an organism showing a dominant trait.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply test-cross principles to determine unknown genotypes.

questions.prompt: In the ABO blood group system, a person with genotype IAIB has blood group AB. What inheritance pattern is shown?
options: Codominance
Complete dominance of O
Sex linkage only
Polyploidy
questions.correctAnswer: Codominance
questions.explanation: Both IA and IB alleles are expressed together in blood group AB.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply codominance to explain ABO blood group inheritance.

questions.prompt: How can non-disjunction during meiosis affect gametes?
options: Some gametes may receive an extra chromosome or lack one chromosome
Every gamete becomes genetically identical to the parent body cell
All chromosomes disappear from every gamete
The gametes become chloroplasts
questions.correctAnswer: Some gametes may receive an extra chromosome or lack one chromosome
questions.explanation: Failure of chromosomes to separate properly can produce gametes with abnormal chromosome numbers.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse the effect of meiotic errors on chromosome number in gametes.

questions.prompt: A recessive trait appears in a child whose two parents do not show the trait. What is the best genetic explanation?
options: Both parents are carriers of the recessive allele
The child inherited no alleles from either parent
Dominant alleles never appear in parents
The trait must be caused by photosynthesis
questions.correctAnswer: Both parents are carriers of the recessive allele
questions.explanation: Unaffected heterozygous parents can each pass on a recessive allele, producing an affected homozygous recessive child.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse family inheritance patterns for recessive traits.

questions.prompt: A farmer repeatedly breeds only the fastest-growing chickens. Which risk should be considered in this selective breeding programme?
options: Reduced genetic diversity may increase vulnerability to disease
All offspring will immediately become different species
The chickens will stop inheriting genes
Meiosis will no longer occur in the flock
questions.correctAnswer: Reduced genetic diversity may increase vulnerability to disease
questions.explanation: Strong selection for one trait can narrow the gene pool and reduce resilience to disease or environmental change.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse benefits and risks of selective breeding in agriculture.

questions.prompt: Which approach best shows ethical use of genetic screening information in a family health context?
options: Provide counselling, protect privacy, and allow informed decisions
Publish all results publicly to warn neighbours
Use results to shame people with inherited conditions
Force every person with a recessive allele to avoid education
questions.correctAnswer: Provide counselling, protect privacy, and allow informed decisions
questions.explanation: Ethical genetic screening respects privacy, informed consent, and non-discrimination.
questions.learningOutcome: Evaluate ethical considerations in using genetic information.

questions.prompt: A bean breeder wants plants that resist disease and mature early. Which plan is most scientifically sound?
options: Cross parents with the desired traits, screen offspring, and select lines that consistently show both traits
Plant only one seed and assume it contains every useful allele
Ignore inherited variation and choose plants at random forever
Expose harvested beans to bile to create resistance
questions.correctAnswer: Cross parents with the desired traits, screen offspring, and select lines that consistently show both traits
questions.explanation: Breeding combines useful variation and uses repeated selection to stabilise desired inherited traits.
questions.learningOutcome: Design a simple selective breeding strategy using inherited variation.

questions.prompt: In an ecosystem, which organism group makes organic food from inorganic substances using light energy?
options: Producers
Primary consumers
Decomposers
Parasites
questions.correctAnswer: Producers
questions.explanation: Producers such as green plants photosynthesise and form the base of many food chains.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify producers and their role in ecosystems.

questions.prompt: What does ecological niche mean?
options: The role and position of an organism in its ecosystem
The total number of chromosomes in a gamete
The shape of an enzyme active site only
The amount of bile released after a meal
questions.correctAnswer: The role and position of an organism in its ecosystem
questions.explanation: A niche includes how an organism uses resources, interacts with others, and survives in its habitat.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain ecological niche as an organism's functional role in an ecosystem.

questions.prompt: Why are quadrats useful when studying grassland plants?
options: They sample a known area so plant abundance can be estimated
They measure oxygen level in blood directly
They digest leaves before weighing them
They prevent all random sampling
questions.correctAnswer: They sample a known area so plant abundance can be estimated
questions.explanation: Quadrats allow learners to estimate frequency, density, or percentage cover of organisms in a defined area.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain how quadrats are used to estimate distribution and abundance.

questions.prompt: What is the role of nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the nitrogen cycle?
options: They convert atmospheric nitrogen into compounds plants can use
They convert glucose directly into oxygen
They remove all proteins from soil
They digest cellulose in human intestines
questions.correctAnswer: They convert atmospheric nitrogen into compounds plants can use
questions.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria make nitrogen available for plant growth by forming usable nitrogen compounds.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the contribution of microorganisms to nitrogen cycling.

questions.prompt: Why does an energy pyramid usually become narrower at higher trophic levels?
options: Energy is lost as heat, movement, waste, and undigested material at each transfer
Energy is created at each feeding level
Consumers photosynthesise more than producers
Decomposers stop all energy movement
questions.correctAnswer: Energy is lost as heat, movement, waste, and undigested material at each transfer
questions.explanation: Only a fraction of energy passes to the next trophic level, so less biomass can be supported higher up.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply energy-transfer ideas to explain pyramid shape in ecosystems.

questions.prompt: Fertiliser runoff enters a pond and is followed by algal bloom and fish deaths. What process best explains this sequence?
options: Eutrophication
Meiosis
Osmoregulation
Translocation
questions.correctAnswer: Eutrophication
questions.explanation: Excess nutrients stimulate algal growth; decomposition later reduces oxygen and can kill aquatic animals.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply ecological knowledge to explain effects of nutrient pollution.

questions.prompt: In a mark-release-recapture study, 40 beetles are marked and released. Later, 50 beetles are captured and 10 are marked. What is the estimated population?
options: 200 beetles
100 beetles
80 beetles
20 beetles
questions.correctAnswer: 200 beetles
questions.explanation: Estimated population equals first marked times second catch divided by recaptured marked: 40 x 50 divided by 10 equals 200.
questions.learningOutcome: Calculate population estimates using mark-release-recapture data.

questions.prompt: How does misuse of antibiotics promote resistant bacterial populations?
options: Susceptible bacteria die while resistant bacteria survive and reproduce
Antibiotics make every bacterium photosynthesise
Resistant bacteria stop passing DNA to offspring
Antibiotics convert bacteria into human cells
questions.correctAnswer: Susceptible bacteria die while resistant bacteria survive and reproduce
questions.explanation: Antibiotic pressure selects for bacteria with resistance traits, increasing their frequency over generations.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse antibiotic resistance as an example of natural selection.

questions.prompt: Which conservation plan best combines biodiversity protection with community benefit near a Kenyan forest?
options: Support controlled community forest use, habitat restoration, and monitoring of key species
Clear the forest for short-term charcoal production only
Remove all local participation from conservation decisions
Introduce any foreign species without ecological assessment
questions.correctAnswer: Support controlled community forest use, habitat restoration, and monitoring of key species
questions.explanation: Sustainable conservation protects habitats while involving communities that depend on ecosystem services.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse conservation strategies that balance ecological and community needs.

questions.prompt: Which student project best measures biodiversity changes along a polluted stream?
options: Sample the same stream sections with a standard method, identify organisms, compare diversity, and record pollution indicators
Visit one point once and count only the largest animal seen
Collect organisms randomly without recording location or water condition
Estimate biodiversity by asking learners to guess species names from memory
questions.correctAnswer: Sample the same stream sections with a standard method, identify organisms, compare diversity, and record pollution indicators
questions.explanation: Reliable biodiversity monitoring uses repeatable sampling, identification, location records, and environmental observations.
questions.learningOutcome: Design a fieldwork plan for assessing biodiversity and environmental change.
